newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Ex-Sweden air cargo rates to Asia edge higher.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Sweden air cargo rates to Asia edge higher.

text.p: Air cargo rates from Stockholm were steady in the traditional post-holiday lull, but some routes -- especially to Asia -- showed signs of picking up, a Reuter poll of freight forwarders and airlines showed.
"Prices remain the same but we're planning for an increase from March 1," said Jens Heide, cargo manager Scandinavia and Finland for Singapore Airlines.
"Spot prices have increased. There are cases where we have charged more than our standard rate," he added.
"There have not been many ad hoc shipments because of the space problem in December," said Par Walstedt, of freight forwarder United Air Service.
Lufthansa Cargo AG's planned price increases for the Nordic region had not been finalised, but other airlines could follow, some players said.
"We haven't concluded the final figures yet," said Martin Schlingensiepen, director cargo Northern Europe at Lufthansa Cargo AG.
"But it will mean increases on all the routes from Scandinavia effective March 1, similar to those all over Europe," he added.
Or, it could lead to some freighters leaving the market, which is still considered by many to be overcrowded with capacity by too many regular freight operations.
"Either you pay or we quit, an airline could say. There's still a lot of freight operating from Sweden at the moment," one forwarder said.
Volumes dropped off sharply after a New Year rush as shippers tried to beat a January 1 deadline when Chinese import charges increased.
"We had a few shipments where we took a surcharge because agents asked for express service," said Peter Sull, cargo and mail sales manager for Scandinavia & Finland for Thai Airways .
"December and November are of course the hottest months. It's a normal drop off," Sull added.
"The past two weeks have been non-existant. There have been very few movements here," one forwarder said.
Other players were less optimistic about the possibility of increasing rates this spring hot on the heels of an almost industry-wide fuel surcharge.
"There may be minor adjustments according to the market availability and demand, but I don't see any major moves," said Anders Uddman, British Airways cargo manager for Northern Europe.

"The operating (or fuel) surcharge was implemented by most airlines in November...This has been very hard for the market to swallow. On average it gave something like a five percent increase overall," Uddman told Reuters.
"Because of this I can't see any price increases (this spring), only adjustments," he said.

Rates to the U.S. were mixed compared to in early December, the time of the latest ex-Stockholm air cargo market report. The average rate to New York's JFK rose slightly to 10 crowns per kg from 9.90, for a 100 kg shipment.
To Chicago the rate was steady at 11.20 crowns per kg compared to 11.25 and to Los Angeles it was also flat at 12.70 crowns compared to 12.75.

To the Far East rates showed signs of pushing higher, with an average of 13.40 crowns per kg to Hong Kong compared to 13.30 crowns a month earlier. To Singapore the rate edged up to 13.50 from 13.40 and to Bangkok it ticked up to 13.10 from 13.
To Japan it inched up to 19.65 from 19.55 crowns.
To the Far East players said telecommunications equipment, electronics, spare parts for cars and furs filled bellyholds.
"Lots and lots of mobile telephones from Ericsson to the Far East," was how one forwarder summarized the past month.
Rates to Dubai were static at 10.20 crowns per kg, as were prices to Johannesburg at 20.30 crowns per kg.
To London the rate was more or less steady at 7.55 crowns per kg compared to 7.60 crowns and to Paris it was also unchanged at 7.25 crowns compared to 7.30 crowns.
To Sao Paulo the rate was also flat at 20.80 crowns.
"It's steady from South America. Everything depends on Brazil," said Paul Rudroff, at freight forwarder Wilson & Co AB, which says it has 22 percent of the export market.
Fruit, vegetables and flowers from Brazil often filled returning planes as well as Chilean wine and Colombian flowers, Rudroff said.
"Those flying freighters and not able to get a full load are in the range of 25 to 26 crowns per kg. On passenger flights, it's 27," said a spokesman for one Swedish-based forwarder.
"We run a charter operation between Europe and Sao Paulo and when we do have a return load we can go down to 23 from Brazil," he said.
